# TOP-3383 — Two-prime infinitude, exact digit counting, and the three/four-prime boundary

**Claim type: Literature report.** The official problem asks simultaneously for infinitely many $n$ with $\gcd(\binom{2n}{n},105)=1$ and finitely many with $\gcd(\binom{2n}{n},1155)=1$. The following account proves the digit criterion and exact one-prime counting formula, records the credited infinitude theorem for every pair of odd primes, and checks why a modern low-multiplicity theorem does not establish either requested assertion. No answer to either full assertion is claimed.

Write $B_n=\binom{2n}{n}$ and let $v_p$ be the usual prime valuation. The distinction between odd primes and two matters: $B_n$ is even for every $n\ge1$.

## 1. An elementary proof of the no-carry criterion

For an odd prime $p$, put $h=(p-1)/2$ and write $n=\sum_{j\ge0}a_jp^j$, with $0\le a_j<p$. We claim
\[
p\nmid B_n\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a_j\le h\text{ for every }j.
\tag{1}
\]
Legendre's factorial formula gives
\[
v_p(B_n)=\sum_{\ell\ge1}
\left(\left\lfloor\frac{2n}{p^\ell}\right\rfloor
-2\left\lfloor\frac n{p^\ell}\right\rfloor\right).
\tag{2}
\]
Each summand is either zero or one. If $r_\ell$ is the residue of $n$ between zero and $p^\ell-1$, that summand is $\lfloor2r_\ell/p^\ell\rfloor$.

If every digit is at most $h$, then
\[
r_\ell\le h(1+p+\cdots+p^{\ell-1})=(p^\ell-1)/2.
\]
All terms of (2) vanish. Conversely, if $a_j\ge h+1$ at some position, then
\[
r_{j+1}\ge(h+1)p^j>p^{j+1}/2,
\]
so the $(j+1)$st term in (2) is one. This proves (1) without replacing a valuation by an unjustified digit heuristic.

In particular, avoidance of $105$ means simultaneous restrictions to digits $\{0,1\}$ in base three, $\{0,1,2\}$ in base five and $\{0,1,2,3\}$ in base seven. Avoidance of $1155$ adds the base-eleven digits $\{0,\ldots,5\}$.

## 2. Exact one-prime counts and unconditional sparsity

Allow $n=0$ temporarily. Among $0\le n<p^L$, the number satisfying (1) is exactly
\[
(h+1)^L=\left(\frac{p+1}{2}\right)^L.
\tag{3}
\]
This follows by choosing the $L$ digits independently; leading zeros are included, and excluding zero subtracts one. Equivalently, the indicator generating function is the formal identity
\[
\sum_{\substack{n\ge0\\p\nmid B_n}}z^n
=\prod_{j\ge0}\left(1+z^{p^j}+\cdots+z^{hp^j}\right).
\tag{4}
\]
For each coefficient only finitely many factors matter. Uniqueness of base-$p$ expansion proves the identity; no analytic convergence is assumed.

Set $\delta_p=\log((p+1)/2)/\log p<1$. Choosing $L=\lfloor\log_p X\rfloor+1$ in (3) yields
\[
\#\{1\le n\le X:p\nmid B_n\}=O_p(X^{\delta_p}).
\]
Thus each of the two sets in the prompt has size $O(X^{\log2/\log3})$ up to $X$ and has natural density zero. This is an elementary bound, not a claim of the sharpest known estimate for simultaneous digit restrictions.

Zero density does not imply finiteness. Nor may the one-prime counts in (3) be multiplied as though the base-three, base-five and base-seven digit events were independent. They concern the same integer in different bases.

## 3. The nontrivial two-prime result

Erdős, Graham, Ruzsa and Straus [1, Section 2, the consequence preceding Theorem 1] establish that for every pair of distinct odd primes $p,q$, infinitely many positive integers satisfy
\[
\gcd(B_n,pq)=1.
\tag{5}
\]
Their theorem is a simultaneous digit-restriction result; it is not a Chinese-remainder argument that controls only a finite collection of low digits. The source's broader two-base formulation is not needed here, and no unverified transcription of its auxiliary digit-bound parameters is used.

Consequently every two-prime subproblem obtained by deleting one of $3,5,7$ has infinitely many solutions, even though each such solution set has density zero by Section 2. This supplies a genuine proper-subproblem theorem. It cannot be upgraded to the three-prime assertion by intersecting the three infinite sets: infinitude is not preserved under arbitrary intersections.

The odd-prime restriction in (5) must remain explicit. Formula (2), or its binary no-carry interpretation, shows that $v_2(B_n)\ge1$ whenever $n\ge1$. A sentence about “any two primes” taken without this context would be false if one were two.

## 4. What low multiplicity does and does not provide

Croot, Mousavi and Schmidt [2, Theorem 1] prove a different simultaneous result. For a positive integer $r$, $0<\varepsilon<1/(20r^2)$, and distinct primes $p_i\ge c_0(r,\varepsilon)$, they obtain infinitely many $n$ satisfying
\[
v_{p_i}(B_n)\le\varepsilon\frac{\log n}{\log p_i}
\quad(1\le i\le r).
\tag{6}
\]
The checked PDF is arXiv:2201.11274v2, dated January 2023. Both the sufficiently-large-prime hypothesis and the dependence of its threshold on $\varepsilon$ and $r$ are part of the theorem.

Two separate gaps prevent (6) from proving the $105$ assertion. It does not certify that the particular small primes $3,5,7$ exceed that threshold. Also, for fixed $\varepsilon>0$, its upper bound grows with $n$, so it need not force the integer valuation to be zero. Sending $\varepsilon$ to zero changes the allowed prime threshold and the resulting sequences; it does not produce one sequence avoiding the fixed three primes.

The four-prime finiteness assertion is different again. Neither the elementary sparsity bound nor an existence theorem about low valuations supplies a finite upper cutoff. A finite enumeration would require a proof that no later simultaneous restricted-digit integer exists.

It does not assert a new simultaneous digit theorem, a proof of either $105/1155$ conjecture, or a current-best counting bound. No finite search or program execution is used.
